text: We built an agentic contract review system for negotiating legal contracts. Here is the problem we are solving.
This is what in-house counsel sends back to a vendor. Tracked changes and margin comments, in Word. Writing that first pass takes one to three hours per contract.

Every company has a playbook. For each clause it sets three positions: preferred, fallback, and walk-away. Applying it across forty pages is slow. Risky terms hide inside definitions. And this month's redline has to match what the team accepted last month.

The shortcut is to paste the contract into a chat assistant. Our baseline is stronger than that. Same frontier model. Same playbook. The whole contract in one prompt. It still falls short. Only one point one percent of its redlines carry the full playbook position. On forty-thousand-word contracts its F-one score drops to sixty point three percent. And it cannot write into the Word file.
So we built Playbook Redliner. It starts from two things you already have: the vendor's Word file, and your playbook. Eighteen rules, each with those three positions.
Here is a real hosting and licence agreement from our evaluation set. An SEC filing, with lawyer-labelled answers. We act for Corio, the customer.

First, the document becomes a map: every clause, every section, every defined term. A planner reads that map and assigns each rule to the right sections. Then eighteen drafters go to work, one per rule, six at a time.

Each drafter reads its sections, searches the contract, and resolves defined terms. Before it can propose an edit, the exact text it wants to change must match the document, word for word. Then an independent verifier checks the proposal. It never sees the drafter's reasoning. Findings appear here as they pass.

Nothing is written until a person decides. J and K to move. A to accept. E to edit. R to reject. Watch the liability cap. It was capped at a single transaction. Counsel edits it: a mutual eighteen-month cap, with a one and a half million dollar floor. The other findings get the same treatment.
Accepted wording is saved as precedent. The next contract's cap starts from words the team already approved.
Export writes a new copy of the file. Real tracked changes. Real margin comments that cite the playbook rule. Every untouched paragraph is verified, byte for byte.
It also drafts the issues memo. Walk-away items first. Then the fixes. Then what was checked and left alone.

One test contract hides a trap. The cap says twelve months' Fees. But Fees is defined two sections away, as a small one-off fee. So the cap is nearly worthless. The system follows the definition, flags it, and writes one clean redline. The two decoy clauses are left alone.

Now the results, against that one-prompt baseline. Complete redlines: from one point one percent to fifty-four point seven. On the forty-thousand-word contracts, F-one goes from sixty point three to seventy-five point three. Applied tracked changes: from forty-one point seven to sixty-two point five. And nothing is applied silently. Unsure findings go to a person.

Why measure it this way? Because on short contracts, finding issues was nearly solved. Writing the full redline was not. So we pre-registered the metrics, and a set of long contracts, before running the final system.

What actually moved the numbers? Not more agents. A more precise playbook. Every position written as a checklist. A drafter that commits to one position, in its own words. A verifier that checks element by element. And whole-document search for long contracts.
Give a specialist agent one rule, and it will find a violation. Give it a direction instead of a checklist, and it will write half a redline.
Playbook Redliner. Every number, every trajectory, and every tracked change reproduces from the repository, with one command.
